explanation: PKU results from deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. This deficiency prevents the normal metabolism of phenylalanine, leading to accumulation and conversion to phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate).
keyConcept: PKU: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency → phenylalanine accumulates → converted to phenylketones → intellectual disability if untreated.

explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor, along with oxygen and NADPH. BH4 is also required for tyrosine hydroxylase (dopamine synthesis) and tryptophan hydroxylase (serotonin synthesis).
keyConcept: Phenylalanine hydroxylase: requires BH4, O2, NADPH. BH4 deficiency causes malignant PKU.

explanation: Serine is the major contributor to the one-carbon pool through its conversion to glycine, releasing a methylene group (-CH2-). The methyl group can be transferred to tetrahydrofolate, forming N5,N10-methylene-THF.
keyConcept: One-carbon pool: serine → glycine transfers CH2 to THF. Also from histidine, tryptophan, methionine.

explanation: Methionine is synthesized from homocysteine and serine via methionine synthase (requires B12) and other enzymes. The pathway involves converting homocysteine to methionine using a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate.
keyConcept: Methionine synthesis: homocysteine + serine → methionine (requires B12, folate). Cysteine is made from serine + homocysteine separately.

explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia can result from deficiency of pyridoxine (B6, needed for transsulfuration to cysteine), cobalamin (B12, needed for remethylation to methionine), or folic acid (needed for the folate cycle that donates methyl groups).
keyConcept: Hyperhomocysteinemia: B6, B12, or folate deficiency → elevated homocysteine → cardiovascular risk, neurological issues.

explanation: Muscles of facial expression are derived from the second pharyngeal arch (stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, stapedius, and all muscles of facial expression). The second arch is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
keyConcept: Second pharyngeal arch: muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric. Nerve: CN VII (facial).

explanation: The first somatosensory area receives sensory input from the contralateral body. A lesion causes contralateral hemianesthesia (loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body). The face area is in the lower part, upper limb in middle, and lower limb on the medial surface.
keyConcept: First somatosensory area: postcentral gyrus; lesion → contralateral hemianesthesia (loss of all sensation).
modelAnswer: Contralateral hemianesthesia (loss of sensation on the opposite side of the body). More detailed: loss of fine touch, proprioception, and stereognosis on the contralateral side, particularly affecting the distal parts of limbs more than proximal.

explanation: The first somatosensory area (S1) is located in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe and extends onto the posterior part of the paracentral lobule (representing the lower limb). The face is represented in the lower part near the lateral sulcus.
keyConcept: First somatosensory area: postcentral gyrus + posterior paracentral lobule (leg representation).
modelAnswer: Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe and posterior part of paracentral lobule (medial surface). The body representation is inverted: face near Sylvian fissure, upper limb in middle, trunk higher up, lower limb on medial surface (paracentral lobule).

explanation: The second somatosensory area (S2) is located in the superior lip of the postcentral gyrus, behind the central sulcus, and extends into the parietal operculum. It receives input from S1 and is involved in more complex sensory processing.
keyConcept: Second somatosensory area: superior lip of postcentral gyrus, parietal operculum, near lateral sulcus.
modelAnswer: Superior lip of post-ramus of lateral sulcus behind the central sulcus. It lies in the parietal operculum and extends into the anterior part of insula. Smaller body representation than S1, bilateral representation.

explanation: Area 43 (primary gustatory area) is located in the parietal operculum extending into the anterior part of the insula. It receives taste inputs from the nucleus of the solitary tract via the VPM nucleus of the thalamus.
keyConcept: Area 43: primary gustatory cortex in parietal operculum and anterior insula.
modelAnswer: Parietal operculum extending into the anterior part of insula. This is the primary gustatory area, receiving taste sensation via the thalamus (VPM).

explanation: Areas 5 and 7 are somatosensory association areas. Lesions cause astereognosis (inability to recognize objects by touch) and inability to judge size, shape, and texture of objects despite intact primary sensation.
keyConcept: Areas 5 & 7: somatosensory association cortex; lesion → astereognosis (tactile agnosia).
modelAnswer: Astereognosis - inability to identify objects by touch despite intact primary sensation. The patient cannot recognize the size, shape, or texture of objects placed in their hand.

explanation: The inferior parietal lobule consists of the supramarginal gyrus (around the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus) and the angular gyrus (around the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus).
keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule: supramarginal gyrus + angular gyrus. Part of Wernicke's area for language.
modelAnswer: Supramarginal gyrus (around the ascending ramus of lateral sulcus) and angular gyrus (around the posterior end of superior temporal sulcus).

explanation: Lesion of the inferior parietal lobule (dominant hemisphere) causes receptive (sensory) aphasia - difficulty understanding language. In the non-dominant hemisphere, it causes contralateral hemisensory neglect.
keyConcept: Inferior parietal lobule lesion: dominant hemisphere → receptive aphasia (Wernicke's area connections).
modelAnswer: Receptive aphasia (Wernicke's aphasia) - fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. Patient speaks fluently but cannot understand or produce meaningful language.

explanation: The three speech centers are Broca's area (motor speech, inferior frontal gyrus), Wernicke's area (sensory speech, posterior superior temporal gyrus), and the supplementary motor area (medial frontal gyrus).
keyConcept: Speech centers: Broca's (expressive), Wernicke's (receptive), supplementary motor area (planning).
modelAnswer: 1) Broca's area - pars triangularis and opercularis of inferior frontal gyrus (expressive speech). 2) Wernicke's area - posterior superior temporal gyrus (receptive speech). 3) Supplementary motor area - medial frontal gyrus (speech planning and initiation).

explanation: The primary motor area (area 4) is located in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe and extends onto the anterior part of the paracentral lobule on the medial surface (representing the lower limb).
keyConcept: Primary motor area: precentral gyrus + anterior paracentral lobule (leg). Body representation is inverted.
modelAnswer: Precentral gyrus of frontal lobe and anterior part of paracentral lobule (medial surface). Representation is upside-down and contralateral: face near lateral sulcus, upper limb above, trunk, lower limb on medial surface.

explanation: The premotor area has body representation that is upside down and contralateral, similar to the primary motor area. However, the representation is disproportionate - areas requiring skilled movements (hands, face, tongue) have larger representations.
keyConcept: Premotor area body map: inverted, contralateral, disproportionate (larger for skilled movements).
modelAnswer: Upside down, contralateral, and the representation is proportionate to skill - larger areas for hands, face, and tongue (requiring fine skilled movements) and smaller areas for trunk and proximal limbs.

explanation: Lesion of Area 4 (primary motor cortex) causes contralateral hemiplegia, most affecting fine skilled movements of the distal limbs. The face and hand representations are most affected due to their large cortical areas.
keyConcept: Area 4 lesion: contralateral hemiplegia, especially fine movements (face, hand). UMN signs below lesion.
modelAnswer: Contralateral hemiplegia especially affecting fine skilled movements. The paralysis is most pronounced in the distal parts of the contralateral limbs (especially hand and foot), with spasticity and hyperreflexia (upper motor neuron signs).

explanation: The premotor area (area 6) is located in front of area 4, extending across the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri and onto the medial surface of the hemisphere. It programs movements without direct cortical input to motor neurons.
keyConcept: Premotor area: in front of area 4, superior/middle/inferior frontal gyri and medial surface.
modelAnswer: In front of area 4, in the superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri, and on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere. It lies anterior to the precentral gyrus.

explanation: Area 6 lesion causes apraxia (inability to perform learned movements on command), muscle spasticity (due to release of area 4 from premotor facilitation), and reappearance of primitive grasp reflex. Motor learning is impaired.
keyConcept: Area 6 lesion: apraxia, spasticity (UMN release signs), reappearance of primitive reflexes.
modelAnswer: Apraxia (inability to perform coordinated voluntary movements despite intact motor and sensory systems), spasticity of muscles (due to loss of premotor area inhibition on area 4), and reappearance of primitive reflexes like the grasp reflex.

explanation: The frontal eye field (area 8) is located in front of area 6, in the middle frontal gyrus and superior frontal gyrus. It controls conjugate eye movements to the opposite side.
keyConcept: Frontal eye field: area 8, in superior and middle frontal gyri (in front of premotor area).
modelAnswer: In the superior and middle frontal gyri, in front of the premotor area (area 6). Controls voluntary conjugate eye movements to the opposite side.

explanation: Area 8 lesion causes ipsilateral deviation of both eyes (inability to look to the opposite side). The eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion because the intact hemisphere drives gaze toward itself.
keyConcept: Area 8 lesion: eyes deviate toward the lesion (ipsilateral), cannot look to opposite side.
modelAnswer: Ipsilateral deviation of both eyes (eyes turn toward the side of the lesion) and inability to turn the eyes to the opposite side. Patient cannot voluntarily look to the opposite side of the lesion.

explanation: Broca's area is located in the pars triangularis and pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. It is the motor speech center, responsible for speech production.
keyConcept: Broca's area: inferior frontal gyrus (pars triangularis + opercularis), dominant hemisphere.
modelAnswer: Pars triangularis and pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere (usually left). This is the motor speech area responsible for expressive language production.

explanation: Lesion of areas 44 and 45 (Broca's area) causes expressive (motor) aphasia - non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension. The patient knows what they want to say but cannot articulate words properly.
keyConcept: Areas 44-45 (Broca's) lesion: expressive aphasia - non-fluent, effortful speech, good comprehension.
modelAnswer: Expressive (motor) aphasia - the patient has difficulty producing speech, speaks in short, effortful phrases, telegraphic speech. Comprehension is preserved. Patient knows what they want to say but cannot articulate properly.

explanation: The supplementary motor area (MII, area 6 on the medial surface) is located in the medial frontal gyrus, anterior to the paracentral lobule. It is involved in speech planning and initiation.
keyConcept: Supplementary motor area: medial frontal gyrus, medial surface of frontal lobe.
modelAnswer: Medial frontal gyrus (medial surface of frontal lobe), anterior to the paracentral lobule. Also called MII or SMA, involved in planning and initiating complex movements including speech.

explanation: Lesion of the supplementary motor area (MII) causes akinetic mutism - a state of decreased initiative and motivation to move or speak. The patient is awake but cannot initiate voluntary movements or speech.
keyConcept: MII lesion: akinetic mutism - awake but no initiative to move or speak.
modelAnswer: Akinetic mutism - a state of decreased motivation and initiative where the patient is awake and alert but shows no desire to move or speak. Speech is sparse, movements are minimal, despite intact motor pathways.

explanation: Pain and temperature from the body: 1st neuron: dorsal root ganglion → spinal cord dorsal horn. 2nd neuron: substantia gelatinosa/lamina 4 → VPL nucleus of thalamus (decussating as spinothalamic tract). 3rd neuron: VPL → somatosensory cortex.
keyConcept: Pain/temp pathway (body): DRG → dorsal horn → VPL (decussates at spinal level) → SI cortex.
modelAnswer: First order neuron: cell body in dorsal root ganglion, peripheral process from receptor, central process enters spinal cord. Second order neuron: substantia gelatinosa (lamina 2) for slow pain; nucleus proprius (lamina 4) for fast pain and temperature. Axons cross at spinal level and ascend in spinothalamic tract to VPL nucleus of thalamus. Third order neuron: VPL nucleus of thalamus to primary somatosensory cortex.

explanation: Pain and temperature from the face: 1st: trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus of trigeminal. 2nd: spinal nucleus → VPM nucleus of thalamus (via quintothalamic tract). 3rd: VPM → somatosensory cortex.
keyConcept: Pain/temp pathway (face): trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus of V → VPM → cortex. Crosses in brainstem.
modelAnswer: First order neuron: cell body in trigeminal ganglion, peripheral process from facial skin/mucosa, central process to spinal nucleus of trigeminal. Second order neuron: spinal nucleus of trigeminal nerve, axons cross as quintothalamic tract to VPM nucleus of thalamus. Third order neuron: VPM nucleus to primary somatosensory cortex (lower face area).

explanation: Crude touch and pressure: 1st: DRG → spinal cord dorsal column. 2nd: nucleus proprius (lamina 4-5) → VPL via anterior spinothalamic tract. 3rd: VPL → somatosensory cortex. This is different from fine touch which travels in dorsal columns.
keyConcept: Crude touch/pressure: DRG → nucleus proprius → VPL (via anterior spinothalamic) → cortex.
modelAnswer: First order neuron: dorsal root ganglion cell, central process to dorsal column. Second order neuron: nucleus proprius (laminae 4-5 of dorsal horn), axons cross and ascend in anterior spinothalamic tract to VPL nucleus of thalamus. Third order neuron: VPL nucleus of thalamus to primary somatosensory cortex.

explanation: The dorsal column tracts (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry epicritic sensations: fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, stereognosis, and two-point discrimination. These are precise, discriminative sensory modalities.
keyConcept: Dorsal columns: fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, stereognosis. Epicritic sensations.
modelAnswer: Fine touch, proprioception (conscious), vibration sense, deep pressure, and stereognosis (recognition of size, shape, and texture of objects). These are discriminative tactile and proprioceptive sensations that require intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.

explanation: Conscious proprioception and fine touch: 1st neuron: DRG → medulla (dorsal columns). 2nd neuron: gracile/cuneate nuclei → VPL via internal arcuate fibers (decussation = sensory decussation). 3rd neuron: VPL → SI cortex.
keyConcept: Conscious proprioception: DRG → gracile/cuneate nuclei → VPL (decussates in medulla) → cortex.
modelAnswer: First order neuron: dorsal root ganglion cell, central process ascends in dorsal column (fasciculus gracilis for lower body, fasciculus cuneatus for upper body) to the medulla. Second order neuron: gracile and cuneate nuclei of medulla, axons cross as internal arcuate fibers (sensory decussation) to form medial lemniscus to VPL nucleus of thalamus. Third order neuron: VPL nucleus of thalamus to primary somatosensory cortex.

explanation: The four tracts carrying unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum are: posterior spinocerebellar (lower limb, from Clarke's column), anterior spinocerebellar (both limbs, from spinal border cells), spino-olivary (to inferior olive then cerebellum), and cuneocerebellar (upper limb, from accessory cuneate nucleus).
keyConcept: Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum: posterior and anterior spinocerebellar, spino-olivary, cuneocerebellar tracts.
modelAnswer: 1) Posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's column, lower limb). 2) Anterior spinocerebellar tract (from spinal border cells, both limbs). 3) Spino-olivary tract (to inferior olivary nucleus, then to cerebellum). 4) Cuneocerebellar tract (from accessory cuneate nucleus, upper limb).

explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract forms the external arcuate fibers. These fibers arise from the accessory (lateral) cuneate nucleus and enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, carrying unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.
keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract: from accessory cuneate nucleus → external arcuate fibers → cerebellum.
modelAnswer: The cuneocerebellar tract. Its fibers arise from the accessory cuneate nucleus and form the external arcuate fibers that enter the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, carrying unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.

explanation: Unconscious proprioception from the lower limb is carried to the cerebellum by: posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus, T1-L2), anterior spinocerebellar tract (from spinal border cells), and spino-olivary tract (to inferior olive then cerebellum).
keyConcept: Lower limb unconscious proprioception: posterior spinocerebellar, anterior spinocerebellar, spino-olivary tracts.
modelAnswer: 1) Posterior spinocerebellar tract - from Clarke's column (T1-L2) ascends in spinal cord to enter cerebellum via inferior cerebellar peduncle. 2) Anterior spinocerebellar tract - from spinal border cells, ascends and enters via superior cerebellar peduncle (fibers cross back in cerebellum). 3) Spino-olivary tract - synapses in inferior olivary nucleus, then olivocerebellar fibers enter cerebellum.

explanation: The two major extrapyramidal tracts (motor pathways outside the corticospinal tract) are the tectospinal tract (from superior colliculus, controls neck muscles) and the rubrospinal tract (from red nucleus, controls limb flexor muscles).
keyConcept: Extrapyramidal tracts: tectospinal (neck control), rubrospinal (flexor muscles). Both modulate movement.
modelAnswer: 1) Tectospinal tract - originates from superior colliculus, crosses in dorsal tegmental decussation, descends to cervical spinal cord to control neck and upper trunk muscles in response to visual stimuli. 2) Rubrospinal tract - originates from red nucleus, crosses in ventral tegmental decussation, descends to control flexor muscles of the upper limb.

explanation: The olivospinal tract originates from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla. It descends to the spinal cord and is involved in motor learning and coordination, carrying error signals from the olive to the cerebellum via climbing fibers.
keyConcept: Olivospinal tract: from inferior olivary nucleus. The olive receives input from red nucleus and cerebellum.
modelAnswer: Inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla. The inferior olivary nucleus receives input from the red nucleus (rubro-olivary fibers) and cerebellar nuclei, and its efferent fibers form the olivospinal tract and olivocerebellar tract (climbing fibers).
